I just finished my first play through of the game and got what I can assume is the expected good ending. Given the gallery, there seems to be multiple types of endings.

This was... short. Much shorter than 2.

I have about 15 hours in Simulacra 2 while this took 3 hours to finish.

That being said, this was because the puzzles and sleuthing required in Simulacra 2 was more obscure and multiparted than what is presented in 3. The to do list was more hints and solutions than just minor quests this time around as it was more specific and broken into far more steps for greater clarity. This made the game much faster to go through as you almost always knew what to do next and could get huge help from the people you were speaking with. Perhaps this was feedback from how 2 was too obscure and some people felt like they spent hours looking for something entirely not obvious to them so this was added to help with it.

I can see it helping but it made it feel like I really wasnt needed. All these people had literally the answers themselves and all i had was someones phone. Any one else could have figured it out where as in 2 I felt like only I COULD solve it.

The feed has been streamlined and what you unlock instead is barfed at you in large chunks instead of the steady trickle that you get from social media sleuthing like in 2. This however made everything feel less personal. I didnt care about the missing people at all since they had nothing else going for them identity wise. They were footnotes pushed in to move the story along.

There doesnt seem to be a lot of character in this one. Pacing with the characters seem incredibly jarring as you go from casual work associates to suddenly having to answer deep mental health trauma in scenarios that come from left field and not in a natural way. The social media aspects were very lacking as you couldnt explore much except a small town feed.

Its easy to describe a story as 4 acts. The hook, the crescendo, the reveal, then the resolution.

I didnt feel like there was a lot of build up. The hook is the crescendo itself. Going into game knowing people are missing already was not really that interesting. Before I knew it, I found myself collecting pieces to finish the "ritual" to solve the problem. This also did not feel like I was apart of the story or had much agency. All the pieces were given to me because i asked someone nicely. A relationship that was already built by someone I never meet. I take advantage of all his work, his relationships, and his findings, just to ask other people to do the big bits for me. I never perform any of the rituals, I never do any of the fighting, I am way more of a casual observer than someone who held anyone's fate in my hands.

The ending left me really bored as I truly didnt feel what the relationship was between any of the people. The premise is a bit wonky as its a shut in PI type that just made esoteric relationships with various people around town that suddenly become holders of big puzzle pieces.

I am guessing due to pandemic, the development had to cut back because there doesnt seem to be a giant web of possibilities like 2 did, there are very straight cut and dry of live or die decisions and I kept feeling like I could have messed up everything when the wording between two dialogue options were basically the same and you had only 3 seconds to choose.

Some of the UI and UX were confusing. The minigame felt incredibly easy but that made me question if I was getting baited into something but instead it really was just simply as it was presented. It was more tedious than fun because you had to watch some really weird forced acting as you played the truck guy in phasmophobia on a far smaller scale essentially. 

Not as good as 2. Still recommend because it was enjoyable but definitely a weaker production in comparison.

Simulacra 3, developed by Kaigan Games and published by Neon Doctrine, continues the found-phone horror tradition established by its predecessors, delivering an immersive narrative experience centered around digital mystery and psychological suspense. Set in the eerie town of Stonecreek, the game places players in the role of an intern at a local newspaper tasked with assisting investigative journalist Ruby Myers. The central mystery revolves around the disappearance of Paul Castillo, a software developer whose phone becomes the gateway to unraveling the secrets behind his vanishing. By exploring his digital life through texts, photos, videos, and various apps, players are drawn into a chilling tale that combines supernatural elements with a realistic portrayal of modern technology, creating a sense of intimacy and urgency that few horror games achieve.

The gameplay is built around interacting with Paul's smartphone, where every notification, message, and multimedia file serves as a piece of the puzzle. Players navigate through different apps, decode cryptic information, and use hacking mechanics to access deeper layers of the mystery. The real-time progression of events adds tension and immediacy, encouraging quick decisions that influence the unfolding story. This dynamic storytelling approach allows multiple branching endings based on player choices, enhancing replay value and inviting players to revisit the narrative to uncover all possible outcomes. The interface cleverly mimics a real phone’s UI, making the experience feel personal and immersive, as if players are genuinely investigating a missing person’s digital footprint.

Visually, Simulacra 3 stays true to the series' minimalist yet effective design, presenting a realistic smartphone interface filled with authentic-looking apps and multimedia content. The integration of live-action video calls and interactive elements boosts immersion, while the sound design subtly heightens the suspense throughout the investigation. Despite these strengths, some players have found certain puzzles to be ambiguous or overly obscure, which can stall progression and disrupt the narrative flow. The pacing, while deliberately methodical to build atmosphere, may feel slow to those expecting more traditional horror gameplay or quicker resolutions.

Critical reception for Simulacra 3 has been varied, reflecting its niche appeal. While some reviewers praise its atmospheric storytelling, innovative use of the found-phone format, and the effective blend of horror with investigative mechanics, others point out shortcomings in character depth and the occasional frustration with puzzle design. The player community echoes this division, with many appreciating the eerie mood and unique narrative delivery but expressing disappointment over certain gameplay limitations and the game's pacing. For fans of narrative-driven horror and those intrigued by the concept of piecing together stories through digital clues, Simulacra 3 offers a compelling experience, though it may not resonate with everyone.

In summary, Simulacra 3 represents a strong continuation of the found-phone horror genre, delivering a haunting and interactive story that makes clever use of modern technology as a storytelling device. Its immersive atmosphere and branching narrative paths offer a deep dive into mystery and supernatural horror, appealing especially to players who enjoy investigative and choice-driven games. While some gameplay elements and pacing choices might divide opinion, the game stands as a noteworthy title for those looking to explore a psychologically tense and digitally immersive horror experience.

Rating: 6/10

review_text_raw:
Loved the first two games and was very excited to start the third. The prospect of a new setting---getting away from depraved online influencers and into a rural area---seemed neat. And we might even be working against a new threat, be it a new mutation of the Simulacra or perhaps a different monster altogether. 

In the previous two games, you get engaged right away.
 
Game 1 starts with the phone glitching out, emitting eerie sounds the second you touch it. Then, as though haunted, it forcibly opens one video among a dozen corrupted files, showing a brief yet shocking video that teases the main mystery: what happened to Anna and is this phone haunted? The video is fragmented and ambiguous but the victim’s distress is very clear. Her final words? “Don’t come looking for me.” Its immediately intriguing. 

In the second game you're a junior detective at the local precinct. It starts with a meeting between you and the chief, where he confides to you the existence of a secret division within the police department, one which handles unnatural phenomena. He hands you stolen evidence: a phone, from the recently deceased Maya, who's strange death frightened the PD regulars into closing her case prematurely. In light of their unwillingness to discover the truth, the chief tasks you personally with spelunking through the phone to unearth clues. He needs your help because he's an older fellow who's not technologically inclined, while you're the young whippersnapper who's hip with the youths and does the iphones. 

Right away there's a sense of urgency. The department is looking for the stolen evidence, you’re breaking the rules just by having this conversation with the chief, and this secret division desperately needs to furnish some results or risk being shut down by the higher ups. And it’s all up to you.

Like the first installment, there’s some spooky phone glitches which show us something is terribly wrong but doesn’t show us exactly what, baiting the mystery.

To help you along, the chief sets you up with cutting edge, AI based software to help you log clues, disseminate evidence, remote hack the victim’s laptop and restore corrupted files. It was developed to help law enforcement conduct investigations which, in our modern world, are increasingly linked to social technology and personal communications. So it’s at least believable. And it imparts a cool-factor, being given access to exclusive, law enforcement tech.

In game three, you’re just some indistinguishable f*ck from the neighborhood watch group. You’re met with a normal phone and some flat, uninteresting dialogue from Ruby, who decides that the best gambit to enlist your assistance is to belittle you, calling you out as the office coffee b*tch and saying “you might know me, I’m the one who’s always ordering the double tall macchiato” or whatever. As if to imply that you, you loathsome, lowly creature, are so far beneath her station that you could only recognize her by the coffees she sends you to fetch like the obedient mud worm you are.

Then, after nailing down just how useless you are, she inexplicably puts her entire case in your hands. And by “inexplicably,” I mean there’s no reason whatsoever for her to need you or trust you at all. She just heedlessly unloads her project—a project that could very easily get her fired—onto you, who she has just thoroughly disrespected.

You get another scanning tool but unlike the WARDEN app from Simulacra 2, this one feels… shoehorned. It was made by some b*tchless basement dweller named Paul, who looks and acts like a sock puppet, who’s tied his unusual app to the GPS. For reasons.

Like its predecessors, you still get to see a creepy video but its overly long and boring. And entirely too blatant. You get to see the cheesy shadow monster, what’s called “the Beldam” (a dumber name I could not fathom) without any preamble or creativity or teasing. Not only that but you stumble across it like it’s just another YouTube video in the shuffle queue. No spooky glitch, no nameless entity forcing you to look at it. Just.. “oh hey neat.”

Somehow, despite the obviousness of the monster video, when you send it to Ruby she instantly decides to go for a stroll in the very same haunted hallway, alone. Which was so unbelievably obtuse it completely shattered any immersion I’d forced myself to conjure just to make it this far.

To make matters even less interesting, everyone in town already seems to know about the Beldam. It’s on their social media, it’s in their photo reels, one @$$hole even talks about seeing its shape in his latte foam. Seriously, wtf? So there’s nothing special about you discovering its existence. Instead of engaging your morbid curiosity and imagination, it just makes you feel like you’re reading hokey bullcrap about bigfoot in a lowbrow tabloid. 

The real nail in this games’ coffin is: instead of giving us one victim to focus on, who’s distress we can directly witness and care about, we’re hit with a list of missing randos who’s peril is entirely unknown to us. They’re just “missing” y’know… kind of like the plot. 

The only threat it draws our attention to, is that a comically greedy mayor wants to pave over the local farmers market and build a mall. 
Wow. 
Call in the national guard. 
Nothing gets me quaking in my boots like the threat of a shopping mall. 

And even then, it’s just plain text. No video, no room for interpretation or imagination. They just black-and-white spell it out for you. “MaYOr bAd, mAke fARmErs sAD.”

This game completely lacks any of the inspiration and vision that made the prequels special. Feels like a cheap cash grab.

Uninstalled.

After enjoying the first two games I thought I was highly anticipating the release for the 3rd one. Sadly this one falls to deliver  anything close to resembling as a interesting/fun game. Even for  9 dollars, at full price. I feel like I wasted money (not rings of power money though). The phone is completely worthless other than what your supposed to do with it at the time, so it doesn't really feel like discovering a person's phone just kinda getting hand held throughout the game. Seems like they went with less "aps" this time, because you use the same ap (atlas) to get from a map feed to a twitter feed. When I called 911 this time around just nothing happens, instead of some somewhat funny dialogue or something else. 411, or dialing 0 also nothing. Trying to call a few people just has calls getting dropped as well which was always kinda a whatever thing, but it's the little things that keep you kinda engaged in story your telling here.

The two characters in the game are very one dimensional. You even though you have the protagonist's  phone you really don't learn anything of interest about this character outside of his drive to stop the plot of the story.  I didn't feel like I was sneaking a peak into his life with loaded with embarrassing messages from maybe his mom,  cringey selfies he taken, or some random thing he bought or really anything that makes the Protagonist feel like a real character. It felt like all information given was utilized to further the plot which made the game feel much more hollow.  

The only other character that you interact with is also just as bland as the main sadly, despite I think the actress trying very hard to work with very bad writing. (I get the lack of pronouns here, but getting called "ROOK" after I just saved your life like a bunch of times was laughable.) Sadly you don't care about saving any of these people, or this town which really feels like the bulk of work was put into. Basically this town is the main character here... Well it's like trying to save Westeros  without meeting anyone who lived there. No one really gives a crap about it. It's actually such a downgrade from either of the previous two games in this retrospect I'm surprised the same company made this game. 

 Nothing was particularly creepy about this one either, Couple times some creepy things happened while I was searching on the phone but it was very minor. The videos that were supposed to be creepy just looked kinda silly, but I understand it's 9 dollars....and  I'm sure there's quite a bit I missed in my first play though, but honestly I have no desire to go back through and get the other "endings" which endings have typically been very weak for the series anyways... I mean could we actually go somewhere with this? I feel like the developers are just trying to milk what was at first a very engaging dynamic and just throwing it into any pot the can stir here. Can like we be maybe a member of an X-FIles unit and maybe we're getting to the bottom of how all Simulcras originated from? or a literal ton of other directions we can actually take??  Sorry on game 3 just having that your phone/ap can kill people is a played out concept. I feel bad writing this, but this game feels so half-assed and disappointing to me who was a big fan of the series I felt betrayed by what should've been a solid stamp on a decent trilogy here.

review_text_raw:
I really wanted to like this game, I really did. 

I loved the previous Simulacra titles, I loved what they did, how they tackled topics of online life from a very different perspective, I loved the variety of characters and the decisions you got to make about them. And mostly, it was just incredibly fun stalking through someone's phone, through social media, seeing other people react to things in realtime, it wasn't 100% convincing, but it made all of it feel a lot more real. And I loved the feeling of danger when getting in contact and confronting the Entities yourself, it was engaging and scary and amazing storytelling.

All of this is gone here.

Let's start with the concept, the previous titles revolved around some current digital topics, online dating, influencers or predatory games. This game mostly drops the digital. It's a ghost story in a town followed through a Maps-App. There's so many topics that could've fit amazingly - NFT's, VR, AR, even Covid and being forced to be home (which admittedly does come up but in a shallow and meaningless way). But we got a Maps-App and a town-mystery, with themes of power, government, community and the interaction of urban myth and history. This too could potentially have been something interesting, but no. 

The story is maybe the most okay part about this game, the town myth is set up nicely, but quite basic, there are some interesting twists and misdirections, and I loved the part about how all of the events started [spoiler]Amy is just a really cool and interesting character[/spoiler]. But many parts absolutely do not work. Some are really forced like [spoiler]when we have to decieve the poor receptionist and cost her her job because Ruby didn't tell us what she was going to do[/spoiler] and the story also doesn't get nearly enough breathing room to work. Especially because you have to work with different characters and convince them of things, yet you've barely interacted before. It doesn't feel like you're participating in a story but playing a bad puzzle game.

The characters are okay-ish, the one you're interacting most with is Ruby and she's written as though you're meant to form a connection, but I just didn't, I didn't feel that much for her or care that much about her, so the emotional core that's built around her just doesn't work. There are some other characters I liked a lot more like [spoiler]Persephone / Damien and Carin[/spoiler] they're fun interacting with and they have personality, but they're also barely there. And even them are just lame compared to the fun interactions with Murillo or unhinged rants of Aria in Simulacra 2, who just felt like real people, with their own desires, hopes, dreams and delusions.

The horror / scary parts are just completely gone. It's so sad, the previous parts could pull you in so much, through the phone glitching or asking invasive or interesting questions, and create a real sense of dread, but here you don't ever feel in danger, because you never are. How would you feel in danger if the Beldam works by [spoiler]ppl seeing graffiti that wasn't there before, or encountering that eye symbol[/spoiler] which are mostly just tied to the real world. Nothing is i.e. indicating you've forgotten time, like that could've been a great point of tension, like a glitch followed by Ruby calling you and asking where you've been the last days. But nothing interesting or scary happens to you. I'd say the most tense sequence was [spoiler]getting Ruby out of Paul's House[/spoiler] but even there you weren't under time pressure, you didn't have to account for it moving, it wasn't challenging at all. Like [spoiler]electronics drew in the Beldam, her phone could've slowly drawn the Beldam towards her unless you activated something else[/spoiler]. And the Beldam itself isn't scary either. The previous Simulacra were always abstract, unfathomable, which made them scary and interesting, but giving the Beldam a bad CGI form didn't do the "horror" any favors. 

The mechanics in the game and the puzzles were also just lame. Most of it is very bland and unoriginal and the Atlas app (maps) is probably the worst of all. It's such a hacked together mess that doesn't make sense as a piece of software, especially the tracking function, and the hints in that function just make everything a lot worse. Like [spoiler]Thomas favorite place gives you the hint with the coffee order. At first I thought, hey there's this dude rating the Beldam locations, maybe I have to bring that in order? Nope. It says something about chronology, maybe I have to sort the ratings by the date posted? Nope. Oh it says something about a specific order in the description, I saw the post like that (@leftOnRead) might it be the places from which this account posted in order? Nope. What I didn't know was that I wasn't far enough and didn't have the grind, park and bus stop on the map yet.[/spoiler] I wasted so much time because of the hint system trying to solve something I couldn't yet.

The previous titles made you feel smart for figuring stuff out, piecing it together, hacking into things, especially because you had a "real phone", from another person, where you just had to circumvent things, but this game does the horrible mistake of dropping all pretenses. It's not a phone from a person missing, it's a puzzle box by a nerd who doesn't wanna give you straightforward information. There's nothing personal in there. NOTHING. No photos, no chats, everything is locked in his fun juiced up Atlas version. You don't try to outsmart technology to gather hidden intel, you have to get around the tedious roadblocks put in place by the informant - why, exactly? At first it's framed like he only had time to send the phone, but then WHY did he make the effort of hiding everything in these tedious puzzles? Especially when he wanted the information to get out and Ruby able to act. The "social media" (everything you get is the social page on the Atlas app) is sadly also incredibly sparse. There's a few posts you can go through, but where in S2 these mattered and you got to know more about the characters and some characters you would later interact with, here in S3 they barely matter at all. They're not engaging to read through, nor interesting discusssions, they're just lame filler. All of the fun of peeking into someone else's life is gone.

I want to have a small aside about presentation, I guess it was produced under Covid and therefore limited and basically all of it is made with greenscreen and really bad integration. The lighting doesn't match properly, the greenscreen is badly keyed and the acting is okay at best, but these are all things I could've forgiven for an interesting, scary, fun, engaging story. They try to do a lot of 3D stuff where the previous games stuck with 2D effects that worked a lot better, because they don't have the budget to do the 3D right.

Then let's finally come to the ending. Navigating the situation was very confusing. [spoiler]You basically have to talk Ruby down to her senses but I had no idea which answers and which reactions meant what. Sometimes she breaks out in this red demonic voice, but it's unclear if that is supposed to be the entity taking more or getting less control.[/spoiler] I had no idea what was going on and even thought I had failed just to discover I actually got the best ending. All of it is then quickly wrapped up, but it fails to leave anything behind about its themes. Everything is magically fine, or everything is incredibly doomed, it's just as empty as the myth of the Beldam itself. It's really sad to see a series I held in very high regard fall off so steeply.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is back! This series has grown since it first arrived and S3 feels like the biggest game to date. Only slightly longer than previous games, it's a short, contained little story that furthers the Simulacra mythos and gives us a new demon to fight. Once again, the game presents an interesting idea in which society intertwines with technology, using social media, internet, and smart tech to spread rumors, superstitions, and falsities. The Simulacra mythology has always been interesting in it's ability to create a technology-based supernatural horror story that turns out attachment to technology and our internet habits into our biggest dangers and that continues here. 

The gameplay is much the same as previous chapters. This time, however, instead of finding a phone, you're given one by your "partner", who is tasking you with finding the truth behind the disappearance of the phone's original owner and her friend. This, of course, leads into a much bigger mystery. The game has been designed more around PC play, so it seems, and that means production values are bigger and gameplay design is more extensive. Puzzles feel more involving and seem to have more gameplay elements than previous chapters. It's all still fairly straightforward, with puzzles being easy. Dialogue and some action choices continue to drive the game. I will say that I wish more gameplay could have reflected one particular part of the game that felt like it had the biggest and best diversion from the usual for the series. If there is another chapter, I hope that the developers will continue expanding gameplay elements and creating more involved gameplay.

As anyone who has played previous chapters might expect, there's also a lot of not so great elements that have stuck around. The acting continues to leave much to be desired. Considering the low budget, indie nature of the game it's not surprising, nor does it take much away from the experience, but I did find myself chuckling at times when I am sure I was not meant to. There is a lot of campiness here, and that is also in part because of the dialogue. There are also a few grammatical errors that took me out of the game. Overall, I found there to be a certain level of cheese. I also didn't find myself gravitating towards the story like I did previous chapters. There's certainly something interesting about the story here and the focus on yet another aspect of technology and internet culture had a great insight to it, but previous chapters have been more relatable. We've seen a focus on gaming and phone addiction, false internet presence, social media manipulation, and other real world, relatable stories that could feel like they have something very real to say about the player. Expanding the scope here to cover an entire town and having the story's early parts focus on something more supernatural and urban legend-ish created a bit of a disconnect. That is a minor complaint though. I was also a bit disappointed with the ending here. I expected much more from the Simulacra's presence, but it kind of fizzled out in the end. I was hoping for something as effective as S1 and 2, but this one was not quite as scary or intimidating. 

Overall, I enjoyed this chapter. I have embraced the level of camp and very indie production that comes with the game, so getting past that, I can focus on what I enjoy. Those who have enjoyed previous chapters will enjoy this one as well.

review_text_raw: I really enjoyed simulacra 1, pipe dreams, and 2 was honestly really cool. But this isn't it. My biggest peeve with this franchise is that it NEVER continues any kind of overarching story, theres never a bigger picture, they always seem to act like there will be but it never happens. The end of Sim 2 made me think this game would be on a large grand scale, a climax involving the simulacras, but it just fell short and the entire game was predictable. I got the best ending on my first try and it was extremely easy to keep everybody alive, and the other games were difficult to get the best ending. I liked that about the other games, it added mystery and replayability. But this game I got the best outcome on my first attempt without any prior knowledge about anything and that is very disappointing to me and makes me have no desire to really go through it all again. The second game was great because it took me at least a few attempts to get the best ending and I remember being genuinely stumped as to what was going on or whodunnit, but I never felt that with this game. Nothing was a mystery to me, I could see everything coming from a mile away. And there was nothing scary either, just a couple cheap scenes with the phones background and that's it. The first two games the background changes throughout and it makes you feel unsettled and its cool to see, but this game just felt... lazy. It feels like the bare minimum and I was really hoping it would be better, but the reason I didn't want to play this game stood true. I feel like i wasted my time with it, but I do hope if they make another game in this franchise, it's better. I really would like to enjoy the series again, but right now, its just repetitive, nothing new happens, its just the exact same situation in each game and nothing in this world they are creating changes. It doesn't feel like the simulacrums are an actual problem, just a minor inconvenience once in a blue moon. I hope the devs read reviews because I saw a lot of people with similar opinions to mine and I would love to see a sim 4 where something new finally develops in this world their building instead of just same shit different day.

I guess this is my first time ever purchasing a game, then completed the game at the same day (in less than 7 hours). Woah. An achievement. Aside from various games I've tried as playtester. You can watch my full gameplay here https://youtu.be/ez36lTtdP9c or [url=https://www.twitch.tv/videos/1634196168/]here[/url]. In my gameplay, I acquired three good endings: Beldam Rewritten, A Town Reborn, and A New Purpose. I'm also acquired 17/24 achievements, but as everything is in Chinese, I don't know what each achievements means...

Honestly... I'm not that intrigued to purchase the full game after playing the demo. I don't know. Back then it feels like... It lacks something. However, flock of people watching my demo gameplay https://youtu.be/HphgyqpM3VI through my YouTube channel makes me... intrigued, hence I decided to purchase and play the full version. At the same time, I do have enough fund to purchase the game, and it's not that expensive to purchase.
---
For a detective-FMV-esque game... Considering the price, the contents inside, the full duration a player needed to finish the game, I guess... It's priced correctly. It's not too cheap, not too expensive either.

It's clear that the team who developed this game produced-designed-researched-prepared lots of contents to make the game as compelling as possible. How the game tried to keep you as focus as possible also can be seen as how the narration goes, whether from text chats, how the actors acted, voice notes/recordings, and many more. They even included objectives, so for player who probably got lost in the game, could easily check the objectives to stay on the line. Each characters (whether directly communicating with player or no) also have their own distinctive characteristic, and I like it.

The cons probably... Motion sickness. I don't know. I felt dizzy, nauseous, and motion sickness during the video call session with Ruby. Probably as I saw a vertical video moving all the time, yet everything surrounding it are "still". At the same time, as I scroll using my scroll wheel, sometimes it's also makes me feel dizzy, so I have to slow the scrolling speed. Another one... That I don't know if it's actually intentional or no, is the loading speed to choose one out of two options in the final scene, when you video call-ed with Ruby. You have to be SUPER QUICK in deciding what your choice will be, and when the texts were long, you only have like two or three seconds to read and choose. 🤦🏻‍♂️

Aside from those cons, I guess everything is pretty good already. I can't compared this one to previous two predecessor of the same title, SIMULACRA, and SIMULACRA 2, even though I've purchased both months ago when it went on sale. To close, if you have enough money, buy it, and enjoy your 5~6 hours time immersing yourself as a detective in this game.
---
Also.... Damien... DAMIEN... Duh if I'm close with you, I'm gonna kiss you. 💙😚💙

The only character in this game that makes me feel like... He's truly alive. The way he typed, the way he texted, and incorporated those emojisssssss. 💙 Duh I'm head over heels 💙💙💙

Should you play this game?

Have you played the prequels?
No -> Then this game might be fun to try
Yes -> You will be disappointed. 

Let me Break it down:

Horror Elements: Not existent. But it do have tense moments, which makes you feel that there is some kind of adrenaline rushing through your body at some points. But the feeling that this is a horror game is non-existent, you feel the horror story, but the gameplay lack horror elements like the prequels.

Gameplay: if you have played the prequels you are familiar with he puzzles of the game series. This third game, deviates completely from the hard puzzles, and it feels like a game made for Teenagers. The Game feels a lot like it tries to be more user friendly which makes the game feel lacking and not hard or challenging, as it used to be. 
There is still positive aspects of the gameplay as how you progress and play, yet it lacks what makes the game worth, the challenging puzzles and horror elements.
I also do not understand why you get all this help to solve the puzzles. - It is unnecessary, and makes the experience feel lacking. The help is more forced than chosen by the player.

Conclusion: For new players the game might feel decent.The price is high comparing with the games depth and experience.
Do i regret buying it? Yes. - It fails to make me feel scared or challenged as i have experienced with the prequals.

It was... decent to say the least. I liked the part where you had to get your partner out of the building where the Beldam was and the integration of phone calls was pretty neat and helps to move the plot along, although I'd still prefer calls still being just a running gag where you can't talk. But that's where the improvements end, and now lets will get to the setbacks.

The maps integration sucks and I don't like it at all, it also takes the social media and puts it in the map app which has no reason being there, you having to click on a few of the images does not make sense by a technological standpoint like the rest of Simulacra does, and the trial-and-error gameplay of the travel distance is not what Simulacra is about at all. I prefer the music in sim 2 to the audio logs in sim 3, the logs are a one and done while I listened to the songs in sim 2 for months after I finished the game. I fell pretty much nothing for the town in this game unlike the first 2 where the people seem real and you feel for them in the situation they're in, and the climax of the first 2 are fantastic and make you feel like there's really something on the line, but in this game there's really no stakes in the final call at all, it banks on you being hooked to her and the town but it does a lackluster job of hooking you so you feel nothing of note. The ending system where you find out what ending you got and the other endings available has potential, but you can really just hook everything there into 3 endings, bad, meh & good, which just raises the question of, "why not just do what y'all did in the first game?" Also, the amount of scares is just pathetic, it feels like it's building up to something but it never does something, if I recall correctly, there is only one jumpscare in the entire game and it's in the beginning.

After all I bashed this game, I still enjoyed it, and it feels like a mainline Simulacra game and it's more Simulacra than Pipe Dreams will ever be, and the art book gives a lot of information. That being said, Simulacra 2 was better, go play that first and play this with a walkthrough, those travel distance puzzels are impossible to get through on your own. Anyways, thanks for reading this!

[Review after completing 100% of current content]

This is a game marred by a clear disconnect between what narrative the audience expects, and what the creators want to tell. The original horror executed its concept well with its meta elements that weren't present in this new experience turned "deep narrative" about the gentrification of a small community. Remembering its roots, I could count the amount of horror moments in Simulacra 3 with a single-fingered hand. Rook-your character-crumpling like paper could certainly be seen as horror, with his flimsy attempts to push consequences on those around him.

The puzzles felt immature and insulting at best, while tedious and hintless at worst. These ranging from reading two posts on their limited feed to tracing paths that were directly communicated; a confusing case with reviews mentioning the need to "pay close attention." Surprises in narrative were few and far between, boiling down to the Simulacra coming in like a disappointing WWE wrestler that you wished wasn't part of the new arc. Pushed by "Big Horror" in an otherwise new space.

The mixed art form in the single truly interactive camera segment was exciting, teasing more diverse gameplay segments. Pity. That was all. Truly, a pity, with the acting of Ruby and Paul being a joy to see, reminding me of passionate youth theatre. It fell quickly back to its trudging phone interface that felt like a nightmare for subsequent playthroughs. Getting all the ending cards felt like a punishment rather than a reward.

Please purge your mind of previous entries if you're going to give this a go, and be ready to spend more time reading meaningless social feeds to fish for info used in two more obtuse puzzles. Keep in mind, this remains the most expensive entry in the series.

I'm giving this a positive review because it's still an enjoyable game, but if you're a massive fan of the previous Simulacra games like I am, you may be pretty disappointed by Simulacra 3. The overall design is fine, and the puzzles are fun, even if this game feels significantly easier than the previous Simulacra games (I mean it's really easy to get the good ending on your first try... you'd practically have to be expressly trying in order to not get it).

The worst part of the game is [spoiler]the fact that it's not really a simulacra at all. It's basically just a regular ghost that they're calling a simulacra for some reason. It's not attached to an app or any sort of technology at all. It deviates from the entire idea of the Simulacra series and feels like it doesn't deserve to be a part of the series[/spoiler].

The characters also have much less personality in this game and feel boring compared to the previous games. You never get to know Paul well like you did with Anna and Maya in Simulacra 1 and 2.

[spoiler]The ending scene where you confront the simulacra is also a huge step back from the previous games. In the others, you interact with it directly, and it feels intense and immersive. In Simulacra 3, you're only interacting with it through someone else, and you feel quite removed from the action. These scenes are always the climax of a Simulacra game, so that's quite disappointing.[/spoiler]

Like all previous Simulacra games, Simulacra 3 has multiple endings, but they're just presented as text blurbs at the end, which feels like really cheap and lackluster storytelling, especially for a studio as brilliant as Kaigan Games. I 100%ed all other Simulacra games, including Pipe Dreams, which is pretty hardcore to 100%, but I just didn't have any motivation to do the same with Simulacra 3. If they allowed you to restart the game at particular checkpoints, I would've, but I don't want to play through the entire game again just for some different ending texts and a few achievements that don't feel worth it.

I think this would've been a perfectly great game if it hadn't been tied to the Simulacra series. If Kaigan Games wants to experiment with other types of stories, that's fine, but they taint the new game and the Simulacra series alike when they try to tie them together. Basically, if you're a Simulacra fan, don't treat this as a Simulacra game.

On it's own, this is a good game. Compared to its' predecessors it's arguably lacking, but I think moreso because of the expectations the first two created for the player. 

This game is absolutely less jarring, intense, and/or scary than the first two. The story is dark and there are some creepy videos but at no point was I reeling back from my monitor like the other games. 

There are new mechanics, such as an interactive map with some interesting functionality and a camera surveillance mini-game, but overall it definitely feels like a Simulacra game. The puzzles are relatively straight forward although I did get stuck once or twice, and to be fair difficulty is highly subjective.
